notes.meaning: Mordecai learned about the wicked decree to destroy all the Jews across the empire. In his deep sorrow, he tore his clothing, put on rough sackcloth and ashes, and cried out loudly through the city streets. This was an ancient way to openly express heartbreak and alert others to a great danger.

Mordecai walked only as far as the palace gate, because Persian law strictly forbade anyone wearing mourning clothes from entering. The king wanted to keep sadness, trouble, and bad news far away from his royal sight. An earthly king can shut out the sight of grief, but he cannot stop real suffering or death.

As the royal order was read throughout every province, the Jewish people were thrown into deep distress. They cried out, wept bitterly, went without food, and lay on rough cloth and ashes on the bare ground. Even though God's name is not directly mentioned here, their fasting showed they were humbling themselves and begging the Lord to step in.

Esther's maids and palace attendants told her that Mordecai was sitting outside the gate in sackcloth, which deeply troubled her. She sent him proper clothes so he could take off his mourning outfit and return to his duties, but he refused to accept them. Mordecai would not act like everything was normal while his entire nation was marked for slaughter.

Esther called for Hathach, a trusted royal servant assigned to assist her, and sent him out to Mordecai. She needed to learn the real reason behind Mordecai's extreme grief. Because Persian queens were kept private inside the harem, she had to rely on a messenger to communicate with the outside world.

Hathach went out to find Mordecai in the public square in front of the royal palace gate. This open city square was where citizens gathered and official business was conducted. There, Hathach could speak with Mordecai and receive his message.

Mordecai explained the whole situation to Hathach, including his conflict with Haman. He also named the exact amount of silver Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to wipe out the Jews. This huge sum showed just how determined and greedy Haman was to destroy them all.

Mordecai gave Hathach an official copy of the written decree that ordered the killing of the Jews in Susa. He charged the servant to show it to Esther and urge her to go directly to the king to beg for mercy for her people. Mordecai wanted her to see the actual royal decree so she would understand that immediate action was required.

Hathach returned to the palace and reported Mordecai's full message to Queen Esther. He told her about the cruel decree and the urgent request for her to intervene with the king. Esther was now forced to face the deadly danger threatening her people.

Esther gave Hathach another message to carry back outside to Mordecai. Because she could not leave her quarters to talk in person, this royal servant served as their private link. Her reply was meant to explain why Mordecai's request was so dangerous.

Esther reminded Mordecai that everyone in the empire knew the king's strict law about uninvited visitors. Anyone who walked into the king's inner court without being summoned was put to death, unless the king held out his gold royal staff to spare them. Since the king had not called for Esther in thirty days, stepping forward meant risking her life.

The messengers went back and reported Esther's words to Mordecai. They described her deep hesitation and the mortal danger she faced under Persian law. This placed the burden of deciding what to do back upon Mordecai.

Mordecai sent back a sobering reply, warning Esther not to think that living in the palace would keep her safe. If the decree was carried out, her identity as a Jew would eventually be known, and she would be killed like the rest. In a crisis, high position and palace walls cannot protect us from shared danger.

Mordecai stated with great confidence that if Esther stayed silent, rescue for the Jews would still arise from another place. He believed God would keep His promises and never let His people be wiped out, but warned that Esther and her family would perish if she failed to help. He suggested that God in His quiet plan had elevated her to royalty for this very moment.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars read the phrase as a question expecting the answer 'no,' taking Mordecai to mean that if Esther does not act, no help will come from anywhere else.

notes.meaning: Esther listened to Mordecai's challenge and made up her mind to act. She sent a final message back with clear instructions for him and the Jewish community. Her fear turned into bold determination.

Esther told Mordecai to assemble all the Jews in the city to fast with her, taking neither food nor water for three full days and nights. She and her female attendants promised to fast the exact same way before she broke the law by going to the king uninvited. Her famous words show that she placed her future entirely into God's hands, ready to die if that was what it cost to rescue her people.

Mordecai left the palace gate and carefully carried out everything Esther asked him to do. He gathered the Jewish people in Susa and led them in the three-day fast. He trusted her courageous leadership and joined the community in seeking divine help.
